lessons.title: Same List, Two Names
lessons.hook: Two names, one list — this is where side effects sneak in.

blocks.heading: One List, Two Names
blocks.body: When you assign one list to a new name, you don't get a fresh list — you get a second name pointing at the same one. Change it through either name, and both show the change, because there's only one list underneath. Passing a list into a function works the same way: the function receives that same list, not a duplicate, so anything it appends or removes inside stays changed after the function returns. Want a real, independent copy instead? Ask for one explicitly, with list(original) or original[:]. Numbers and strings don't have this problem — reassigning them just makes a new value. Lists, dictionaries and sets do, because they can change in place.

blocks.code:
original = [1, 2, 3]
other = original
other.append(4)
print(original)
print(other)
blocks.caption: One list, two names, one change shows through both.

blocks.code:
def add_bonus(scores):
    scores.append(100)
    return scores

class_scores = [70, 85, 90]
updated = add_bonus(class_scores)
print(class_scores)

safe_scores = [70, 85, 90]
protected = add_bonus(safe_scores[:])
print(safe_scores)

steps.say: Appending inside the function changes the actual list the caller passed in, not a private copy.
class_scores and scores are two names for the same list, so the append shows up here too.
Slicing with [:] builds a brand new list, so the function can't touch the original.
safe_scores stays as it was, because add_bonus only saw the copy, never the real one.

blocks.caption: One function, two calls: one mutates the caller, one doesn't.

blocks.code:
def double_first(nums):
    nums[0] = nums[0] * 2
    return nums

prices = [10, 20, 30]
double_first(prices)
print(prices)
blocks.hint: Look at what nums[0] actually is inside the function — is it a copy?
blocks.explain: nums and prices name the same list, so mutating nums[0] inside the function changes prices too.

blocks.prompt: Write remove_last(items) that returns a new list with every item except the last one. Do not change the list you were given — build the copy with slicing. Example: remove_last([1, 2, 3]) returns [1, 2].
blocks.hint: Slicing builds a brand new list — indexing or popping does not.
blocks.explain: items[:-1] copies every item except the last into a new list, leaving items untouched.

bullets: Assigning a list to a new name shares the same list, not a copy.
A function parameter is another name for the list you passed in.
Slicing or list() makes a real, independent copy when you need one.
blocks.remember: Two names, one list, until you deliberately copy it.

blocks.say: Time for a real one — go work an angle where a copy has to survive the call.

lessons.exitLine: Go put it to work on a real rep.

lessons.title: Stop At The First Match
lessons.hook: Most searches are over the second you find what you needed.

blocks.heading: Find it, then stop looking
blocks.body: To find something in a list, look at each item in order from the start. The instant you find a match, stop and report where it was — checking what's left after that is wasted work. If all you need is a plain yes or no, or the first spot a value shows up, Python's `in` and `.index()` already do that exact walk for you, and they stop the moment they hit too. Reach for your own loop only when you need something extra along the way, like a count, a running total, or a custom rule for what counts as a match.

blocks.code:
temps = [5, 3, -2, 8]
print(-2 in temps)

found = False
for t in temps:
    if t == -2:
        found = True
        break
print(found)
blocks.caption: Same answer either way — `in` already does the walk on the left.

steps.say: Walk from the front, in order, so the first free seat you meet really is the first one.
Test each seat only when you reach it; peeking ahead would break what first even means.
Return the position right away and the walk stops there, with the rest of the row untouched.
Only fall through to here once every seat came back taken.

blocks.caption: A row of seats, checked left to right, until one comes back free.

blocks.prompt: A list holds every scan code a warehouse logged today, in the order they arrived. You need to know how many of them start with "RX". Which tool does the job?
options: in, because it already walks the whole list for you
.index(), because it returns where the first match sits
A loop you write yourself, because nothing built in counts a custom match
Nothing works; a list cannot be searched for part of a value
why: in only ever answers yes or no, and a count is neither of those.
.index() hands back one position and then stops; it never sees the rest.
Right — a count with a rule of its own needs work on every step, which is exactly when you write the walk.
Every value in the list can be tested however you like; the question is only which tool does the testing.
blocks.hint: Ask what each built-in actually hands back, then compare that with what a count needs.
blocks.explain: Both built-ins stop at their answer: one a yes or no, one a position. A count has to look at every item and apply a rule of its own, so this is the case your own loop was saved for.

blocks.prompt: Write `first_passing(scores)`. It returns the index of the first score that is 60 or higher. If none qualify, return -1.
blocks.hint: Loop with the index, test the condition, and return the moment it's true.
blocks.explain: Walking from index 0 and returning right away finds the first qualifying score without checking any others; falling through the whole loop means nothing matched, so -1 is correct.

bullets: Scan from the start; stop the second you find a match.
Reach for in or .index() when you just need yes or no.
Write your own loop only when you need more than that.
blocks.remember: The built-in already stops early; don't rewrite the walk yourself.

blocks.say: Real rep next: build binary search and bubble sort yourself, then pick the right one.

lessons.exitLine: Time for a real rep: build one of these searches yourself.

lessons.title: One Function, Two Answers
lessons.hook: A function that returns two things beats two functions that don't talk to each other.

blocks.heading: Return more than one value
blocks.body: A function normally hands back one value. Sometimes the real answer to a question is two or three things at once — a name split in half, a total and a count. Return more than one value by separating them with commas: return a, b. Python packs them into a tuple without you asking for one. On the calling side, catch them the same way you already unpack any tuple: x, y = the_call(). Each name grabs its matching value in the order it came back. No import, no new type — just more values after return, and more names catching them.

blocks.code:
def split_name(full):
    first, last = full.split(" ", 1)
    return first, last

first, last = split_name("Nadia Karim")
print(last + ", " + first)
blocks.caption: Two values came back. Printing them out of order is the proof they really came apart.

blocks.code:
def line_total(order):
    return order["item"], order["qty"] * order["price"]

def summarize(orders):
    total = 0
    count = 0
    for order in orders:
        item, subtotal = line_total(order)
        total += subtotal
        count += 1
    return total, count

orders = [{"item": "Pen", "qty": 3, "price": 2}, {"item": "Mug", "qty": 1, "price": 8}]
grand_total, line_count = summarize(orders)
print(grand_total, line_count)

steps.say: line_total owns one record's math, so summarize never repeats that formula.
summarize takes the whole list, keeping per-record logic separate from the running total.
Unpacking here names both parts so the loop never confuses the item with its subtotal.
Returning total and count together saves the caller from looping twice for two answers.
Unpacking the call matches names to values in the same order they were returned.

blocks.caption: One helper returns a pair; the loop unpacks it every time through.

blocks.prompt: This function returns two numbers from one list. What does the last line print?
blocks.hint: Check which value the return statement lists first, then match it to the name that unpacks first.
blocks.explain: min(prices) is 4 and max(prices) is 12; low unpacks the first returned value and high the second, so it prints "4 12".

blocks.prompt: Write `totals(records)`. Each record is a dict with `hours` and `rate`. Return a tuple `(total_hours, total_pay)` — the sum of every record's hours, and the sum of every record's hours times rate. An empty list returns `(0, 0)`.
blocks.referenceSolution:
def totals(records):
    total_hours = 0
    total_pay = 0
    for r in records:
        total_hours += r["hours"]
        total_pay += r["hours"] * r["rate"]
    return total_hours, total_pay
blocks.hint: Add every record's hours to one running total and hours times rate to another as you loop.
blocks.explain: Each record adds its hours to the first total and hours times rate to the second; an empty list never enters the loop, so both stay zero.

bullets: A function can return several values packed in one tuple.
Unpack a returned tuple into named variables in one line.
Loop over records, pulling each one's tuple apart as needed.
blocks.remember: Return many values as one tuple — unpack them by position, not guesswork.

blocks.say: Next up: pull two answers out of one function, using real records instead of examples.

lessons.exitLine: Go turn a list of records into answers only your function can give.

lessons.title: Reading a CSV without crashing
lessons.hook: One blank cell in a file, and a careless script dies right there.

blocks.heading: Rows become dictionaries
blocks.body: A CSV file is rows of text with commas between values, and the first row usually names each column. Python's csv module can hand you each row as a plain list, but csv.DictReader upgrades that: it reads the header once and turns every later row into a dictionary, so you pull a value by column name instead of counting commas. Real files are messy — a shopper skips a field, a price cell is left blank. If you assume every field holds a number and convert it, that one blank cell crashes the whole read. Check what actually came back before you trust it, and skip or replace an empty field instead of letting it blow up your program.

blocks.code:
import csv, io

text = "name,price\nApple,1.50\nBanana,0.75\n"
reader = csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(text))
for row in reader:
    print(row["name"], row["price"])
blocks.caption: Each row comes back keyed by header name, not by position.

blocks.code:
import csv, io

text = "item,price\nMask,2.50\nGloves,\nWipes,1.20\n"
reader = csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(text))
total = 0.0
skipped = 0
for row in reader:
    price = row["price"].strip()
    if price == "":
        skipped += 1
        continue
    total += float(price)
print(round(total, 2))
print(skipped)

steps.say: DictReader turns the header row into keys, so you look values up by name, not position.
Stripping the field catches a blank cell that reads as empty text, not a missing key.
Checking for empty text before converting stops a blank row from crashing the whole read.
Only a value that passed the check gets turned into a number, so bad data cannot break the loop.

blocks.caption: Guard the field, then convert it — never the other way round.

blocks.prompt: Read this script mentally, then say exactly what it prints, line by line.
blocks.code:
import csv, io

text = "day,temp\nMon,72\nTue,\nWed,68\n"
reader = csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(text))
total = 0
skipped = 0
for row in reader:
    temp = row["temp"].strip()
    if temp == "":
        skipped += 1
        continue
    total += int(temp)
print(total)
print(skipped)
blocks.hint: Trace each row: does the guard let a blank field reach the conversion?
blocks.explain: Tuesday's blank field never reaches int(), so only 72 and 68 get added — one row skipped.

blocks.prompt: Write total_price(text): it takes csv text with header item,price and returns the sum of the valid prices as a float, skipping any row whose price is blank.
blocks.hint: Read the text with csv.DictReader, then guard the price field the same way the worked example did.
blocks.explain: Skipping a blank field before converting is what keeps one row from crashing the whole read.

bullets: DictReader keys each row by the header, not by position.
Check a field before converting it, so blanks cannot crash the read.
A guard skips one bad row instead of stopping the whole file.
blocks.remember: A file only crashes you if you never look at what actually came back.

blocks.say: Next you'll clean a full file that's built to break naive code.

lessons.exitLine: Go turn a messy file into numbers that hold up.
